lead: A fire detection system watches the engine, APU, cargo holds and toilets for heat, flame or smoke. It raises a cockpit warning, and the crew then releases a stored extinguishing agent into the affected zone. It exists because a fire in a hidden compartment can grow faster than the crew can see it. Fast detection, low false alarms and one reliable discharge path are the whole design aim. Every transport aircraft carries such a system; the same logic protects the APU and the cargo hold.
prereq: You need the engine and APU zone layout from engine fuel and lubricating systems, and basic circuit ideas from Unit 3.

blocks.text: Fire protection has two separate jobs. Detection watches a zone and decides that a fire exists. Extinguishing carries agent to that zone. The two jobs meet at the control unit and the cockpit. A smoke detector in a cargo hold does not put out a fire; it only starts the warning chain.

items: Fast response: the detector must signal within seconds of a flame or a temperature rise, before the fire spreads.
Low false alarms: a warning that cries wolf makes the crew ignore a real fire. The control unit uses a short confirmation delay and compares more than one sensor where possible.
Full zone coverage: no shadow area. A continuous loop or several spot detectors are placed so that any fire in the zone heats at least one sensor.
Testable and resettable: a test switch simulates a detector. After the test the system must return to normal without replacing parts.
Fault indication: a broken wire or a failed detector must show as a fault, not as a healthy zone or as a fire.
Survive the environment: vibration, heat, fuel, oil and cleaning fluids.

blocks.text: The detector is chosen for the zone. An engine nacelle has airflow and hot metal; a cargo hold has boxes and possible smouldering. One detector type does not fit all.

items: Thermocouple: a junction of two metals produces a small voltage when heated. The control unit reads the millivolts. It responds to a fire's heat, not to smoke.
Bimetallic spot detector: two metals with different expansion bend a strip. At a set temperature the strip closes a contact. It protects one small point.

Continuous loop: a tube runs around the zone. In a Kidde loop, heat melts a eutectic salt and the resistance between the central wire and the tube falls. In a Fenwal loop, heat raises the gas pressure inside the tube and operates a switch. The loop covers the whole zone and has no shadow.

Ultraviolet and infrared flame detectors: a UV cell sees the ultraviolet light of a flame; an IR sensor sees its infrared radiation. They respond in under a second. They are paired so that sunlight or a hot brake does not cause a false alarm.

Smoke detectors: an ionisation detector uses a radioactive source to ionise air; smoke reduces the tiny current. An optical detector shines light into a chamber; smoke scatters the light into a photocell. Both suit cargo holds and toilets, where smoke arrives before flame.
Carbon monoxide detector: an electrochemical cell gives a current proportional to CO. It catches a slow, smouldering fire that makes little visible smoke.

blocks.text: The control unit supplies power, watches the loops and decides. It applies a short delay to reject a transient, drives the warning light and bell, and stores a fault code. The test switch injects a simulated detector signal. Crews test the loops before flight; the system then resets.

Engine and APU zones usually have two identical loops, an A loop and a B loop. A fire sensed on either loop gives a warning. A break in one loop gives a fault, while the other loop still protects the zone. That is why the control unit can show FIRE, FAULT or normal, and why a single broken wire does not lose protection.

When the control unit confirms a fire, the cockpit gets a red fire light and a bell. The crew identifies the zone. For an engine or APU fire, the pilot pulls the fire handle. Pulling closes the fuel shut-off valve, the hydraulic shut-off valve and the bleed valve, and arms the squib circuit. Rotating the handle then fires the squib. On the ground an APU fire normally trips an automatic APU shutdown and, on many types, an automatic bottle discharge; in flight the crew uses the APU fire handle.

A squib is a small explosive cartridge. It drives a cutter or opens the bottle valve. One squib gives one shot; after firing it is spent. Some installations carry two bottles, or a bottle with two squibs, so the crew can fire a second shot after the first has knocked the fire down.

Engine and APU bottles are fixed in the aircraft structure, not inside the fire zone. The APU bottle sits in the tail cone or aft equipment bay; the engine bottles sit in the fuselage or wing root close to the engine, and pipes carry the agent to nozzles inside the nacelle. Cargo compartments have their own bottles, often several, released by a cargo fire switch. A lavatory has a small bottle with a fusible link: heat melts the link and the agent discharges without a crew action, and a manual port is provided. Portable extinguishers in the cabin are for the crew's immediate use.

The agent volume follows V<sub>a</sub> = C × V<sub>z</sub> ÷ (1 − C), where V<sub>a</sub> is the volume the released vapour must occupy in the zone in m³, C is the design concentration as a fraction, and V<sub>z</sub> is the zone volume in m³. The division by (1 − C) allows for the air that the agent displaces. The simpler V<sub>a</sub> = C × V<sub>z</sub> is often used instead; it ignores that displaced air, and at 6 % the two forms differ by about 6 %. Mass then uses the agent vapour density.

Halon 1301 is a clean agent: it leaves no residue and breaks the combustion chain. It is also an ozone-depleting substance, so newer designs use HFC-125, HFC-227ea or FK-5-1-12. Water mist cools and displaces oxygen; dry powder suits flammable liquid fires; carbon dioxide is not used in occupied spaces because it can suffocate.

examples.question: A cargo compartment has a volume of 40 m³. The design agent concentration is 6 % by volume. The agent vapour density is 6 kg/m³. Calculate the agent volume and the agent mass needed.
steps: Convert the concentration to a fraction: C = 6 % = 0.06.
Agent volume: V<sub>a</sub> = C × V<sub>z</sub> = 0.06 × 40 m³ = 2.4 m³.
Agent mass: m = V<sub>a</sub> × ρ = 2.4 m³ × 6 kg/m³ = 14.4 kg.
examples.answer: The released agent must occupy 2.4 m³ of the zone (as vapour at zone conditions), which needs 14.4 kg of agent stored in the bottle.

traps: Smoke detection is not suppression. A cargo smoke warning starts the chain; the bottles do the extinguishing.
The fire handle has two actions. Pulling isolates and arms; rotating discharges. Writing only 'pull to discharge' loses marks.
A squib is one-shot. A test does not fire the squib; it only tests the circuit.
Halon 1301 does not work mainly by removing oxygen. It breaks the chemical chain, so a low concentration can stop a flame.
Do not forget the loop test before flight. An untested loop can hide a broken wire.

quiz.q: Name four zones protected by fire detection on a typical transport aircraft.
quiz.a: Engine, APU, cargo compartment and lavatory; many types also monitor the wheel well and the avionics bay.

quiz.q: Why does a continuous loop cover a zone better than a single spot detector?
quiz.a: The tube runs around the whole zone. Any local heat changes the loop and is sensed, so there is no shadow area. A spot detector sees only its own small point.

quiz.q: A cargo hold of 30 m³ needs 5 % agent by volume. The agent vapour density is 6 kg/m³. Find the agent mass.
A cargo smoke detector alarms, but no fire is found. Give two design features that reduce such false alarms and explain each.
quiz.a: A confirmation delay in the control unit rejects a short transient such as dust. A second detector or cross-comparison requires two sensors to agree before a warning, so one dusty sensor cannot start the discharge chain.
It is a small explosive cartridge that opens the bottle valve or drives a cutter when fired.

quiz.q: Why is carbon dioxide not used in an occupied cabin?
quiz.a: It displaces oxygen and can suffocate people. It is suitable for an unoccupied compartment, not a cabin with crew or passengers.

quiz.q: The fire handle is pulled but not rotated. Does agent discharge? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Pulling isolates the fuel, hydraulic and bleed supplies and arms the squib circuit. Rotation is the action that fires the squib and discharges the agent.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer cargo holds use fibre-optic linear heat sensing and video smoke detection to cut false alarms. Halon production is phased out under the Montreal Protocol, so HFC and fluoroketone agents are replacing it. Engine fire detectors are moving to combined UV/IR sensors with digital self-test. Search for 'aircraft cargo fire suppression', 'Halon 1301 replacement' and 'continuous loop fire detector'.
